message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Properties**

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.008 u (average; 1.00794 u for natural hydrogen) |
| **Isotopes** | H‑1 (protium, 99.98 %), H‑2 (deuterium, 0.02 %), H‑3 (tritium, trace) |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | 72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| **Molecular form** | Diatomic (H₂) under normal conditions |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| **Density at STP** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (0.00008988 g cm⁻³) |
| **Color** | Colorless |
| **Odor** | Odorless |
| **Taste** | Tasteless |
| **State at room temperature** | Gas |
| **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; forms explosive mixtures with air (2–75 % H₂ in air) |
| **Reactivity** | Forms hydrides with metals; reacts with halogens, oxygen, and acids (forming H₂O, HF, HCl, HBr, HI) |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| **Molecular weight** | 2.016 g mol⁻¹ (for H₂) |
| **Specific heat capacity (gas)** | 28.84 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 298 K) |
| **Thermal conductivity** | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 300 K) |
| **Electrical conductivity** | Very low as a neutral gas; becomes conductive when ionized (plasma) |
| **Magnetic susceptibility** | Diamagnetic (χ ≈ –2.8 × 10⁻⁶ m³ kg⁻¹) |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) |
| **Applications** | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells), rocket propellant, laboratory reagent, metal hydride formation, isotope separation, medical imaging (MRI contrast agents with deuterium/tritium). |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: Only one proton (and usually one electron).
- **Highly reactive**: Forms compounds with almost all elements; key in water, acids, and organic chemistry.
- **Energy carrier**: Combustion releases ~286 kJ mol⁻¹ (energy density ~141 MJ kg⁻¹).
- **Isotopic significance**: Deuterium used in nuclear fusion research; tritium is radioactive (β‑emitter, half‑life ~12.3 y).
- **Physical extremes**: Boils and melts at very low temperatures; extremely low density.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
